implementation_notes: C is the pattern's native ground: POSIX dlopen()/dlsym()/dlclose() is exactly the linking facility the configurator needs, but everything around it - the configuration-script parser, the component table, the init/fini symbol lookup and the unlink order - is hand-written, which is why the support level is manual rather than library. The usual structure is a table of {name, handle, ops} entries: the configurator dlopen()s each script entry with RTLD_NOW so missing symbols fail at load time, dlsym()s the component's entry points, stores them, and calls init(); unlink walks the table in reverse order, calls the stored fini() and dlclose()s the handle. dlclose() only unloads when the reference count reaches zero and no other object still needs the library's symbols, so RTLD_NODELETE (never unload this component) and dlmopen() namespaces (isolate it) are the two escape hatches worth knowing before you design the teardown path.
pitfalls: dlsym() returns NULL both when the symbol is absent and when it is present with a NULL value; call dlerror() (after clearing it) to distinguish the two, otherwise a component silently registers a null entry point.

dlclose() decrements a reference count and only unloads when it reaches zero and no other object still needs the library's symbols, so a component loaded with RTLD_GLOBAL - or whose symbols another library resolved - stays mapped and keeps its state even after it was 'unlinked'.
Unlinking while threads still hold function pointers or registered callbacks into the library is a use-after-free; drain registrations and join threads before dlclose(), in reverse dependency order.

Static TLS and destructor ordering make unloading dangerous for libraries that own thread-local state or C++ static objects; RTLD_NODELETE avoids the crash at the price of never reclaiming the library.
